children: Few leaders leave office so defeated yet still remain relevant a generation later. Tung Chee-hwa, the financial hub's first chief executive who took over after British rule in 1997, has died aged 89. He will largely be remembered for his failed reforms. But as Hong Kong readies its debut five-year economic plan, the city looks set to embrace his ideas and vision.

A former shipping magnate, Tung lost almost every defining battle during his tenure. His landmark policy of building more than 85,000 homes a year was meant to curb runaway property prices. But it was derailed by the Asian financial crisis and then the SARS epidemic six years later. Between 1997 and 2003, home values fell more than 65% as unemployment reached a peak of 8.7% during the outbreak. Tung responded by walking back on many policies and kicking off an austerity drive, which gutted welfare spending and civil servant pay.

Public discontent boiled over when his administration tried to push through a national security law, drawing half a million protestors onto the streets and forcing the government to shelve the bill. Tung resigned two years later, halfway through his second term, citing ill health. Since then, no Hong Kong leader has seriously tried to tackle the city's housing crisis.

Meanwhile, Tung's emphasis on fiscal restraint left a lasting mark: Successive administrations remained reluctant to expand social welfare spending, which probably contributed to widespread public dissatisfaction and the civil unrest that boiled over in 2019. His much-hyped Cyberport project, meant to transform Hong Kong into a tech hub, also disappointed. It's a sharp contrast to neighbouring Shenzhen, which has evolved into the innovation powerhouse Tung had hoped to create.

Tung's policy failures will resonate for current chief executive John Lee, who is set to unveil the city's Five-Year Plan for Economic and Social Development next week. Many of its core themes, more housing, building a technology-driven economy and closer alignment with China's development priorities, are aimed at addressing the same challenges Tung tried to tackle. Hong Kong has been home to the world's least affordable housing market for the past 16 consecutive years; the city boasts one of the greatest wealth disparities among developed economies.

Lee may have better luck in realising the goals he helps to set. Tung adopted Beijing's approach of long-term economic planning at a time when Hong Kong still operated under a laissez-faire capitalistic system. If his successor succeeds where he failed, history may prove kinder to the city's first chief executive than his contemporaries.
Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong’s first chief executive after its sovereignty handover to China in July 1997, died on September 8, aged 89.
John Lee, the current chief executive, will announce Hong Kong’s first Five-Year Plan for Economic and Social Development along with his annual policy address on September 16.
